findings.consequent: Sensory evaluation of wooden office space
findings.mechanism: Wood color has a significant impact on sensory evaluation, with lighter colors creating brighter, more relaxing spaces.
findings.quote: showed a significant main effect of wood color, F(2,177) = 6.95, p = 0.001, η² = 0.07, indicating that wood color had a significant impact on sensory evaluation.

findings.mechanism: Lighter colored wood creates spaces perceived as bright, spacious, and relaxing.
findings.quote: significant differences in the visual perception of dark wood-colored (M = 4.65 ± 1.24) and light wood-colored (M = 5.34 ± 0.89) offices, p = 0.002

findings.mechanism: Medium colored wood creates spaces perceived as bright, spacious, and relaxing.
findings.quote: also between dark wood-colored and medium wood-colored (M = 5.28 ± 0.93) offices, p = 0.001.
no significant difference was found between light wood-colored and medium wood-colored wood, p = 0.889.

findings.mechanism: Low-coverage wood spaces are perceived as more aesthetically pleasing and vivid, while too much wood can be constricting.
findings.quote: the visual perception of the low-coverage wooden space (M = 5.38 ± 0.96) being significantly better than that of the high-coverage wooden space (M = 4.83 ± 1.10), F(1,177) = 7.22, p = 0.008, η² = 0.04.

findings.antecedent: Interaction between wood color and wood coverage
findings.quote: the interaction between wood color and wood coverage was not significant, F(2,177) = 1.72, p = 0.182.

findings.mechanism: Lighter colored wood is associated with higher satisfaction, consistent with preferences for bright and relaxing spaces.
findings.quote: statistically significant difference in satisfaction score among the different wood-colored offices, x²(2) = 11.95, p = 0.003

findings.mechanism: Light wood-colored offices (M=5.60) are more satisfying than dark wood-colored offices (M=4.88).
findings.quote: mean rank satisfaction of 105.12 for light wood-colored offices (M = 5.60 ± 1.27)... and 73.27 for dark wood-colored offices (M = 4.88 ± 1.31).

findings.mechanism: Medium wood-colored offices (M=5.48) are more satisfying than dark wood-colored offices (M=4.88).
findings.quote: mean rank satisfaction of... 98.34 for medium wood-colored offices (M = 5.48 ± 1.21) and 73.27 for dark wood-colored offices (M = 4.88 ± 1.31).

findings.mechanism: Low-coverage wood spaces (M=5.66) are more satisfying than high-coverage spaces (M=5.00).
findings.quote: satisfaction in the low-coverage wooden space (M = 5.66 ± 1.09) was statistically significantly higher than the high-coverage wooden space (M = 5.00 ± 1.41) (U = 3,095.00, p = 0.001).

findings.consequent: Usage willingness of wooden office spaces
findings.mechanism: Lighter colored wood is associated with stronger usage willingness, aligning with aesthetic preferences for relaxed and vivid environments.
findings.quote: statistically significant difference in usage willingness score among the different wood-colored offices, x²(2) = 12.93, p = 0.002

findings.mechanism: Light wood-colored offices (M=5.48) are preferred over dark wood-colored offices (M=4.59).
findings.quote: mean rank usage willingness of 105.29 for light wood-colored offices (M = 5.48 ± 1.42)... and 72.31 for dark wood-colored offices (M = 4.59 ± 1.52).

findings.mechanism: Medium wood-colored offices (M=5.36) are preferred over dark wood-colored offices (M=4.59).
findings.quote: mean rank usage willingness of... 99.04 for medium wood-colored offices (M = 5.36 ± 1.32) and 72.31 for dark wood-colored offices (M = 4.59 ± 1.52).

findings.consequent: Usage willingness of wooden office spaces
findings.mechanism: Low-coverage wood spaces (M=5.47) are preferred over high-coverage spaces (M=5.16), possibly due to perceptions of less constriction and better lighting.
findings.quote: usage willingness in the low-coverage wooden space (M = 5.47 ± 1.36) was statistically significantly higher than the high-coverage wooden space (M = 5.16 ± 1.46) (U = 3250.00, p = 0.004).

stimuli.description: Six 35-second videos (720 dpi) showing office spaces with different wood colors (light, medium, dark) and wood coverage (low 12%, high 35%).
Four scene pictures (300 dpi) for each of the six wooden office spaces, showing different angles.

limitations: Lack of consideration of participant population and insufficient diversity within the study sample, limiting generalizability.
The position of wood on wooden furniture was not considered, which may affect attitudes.
Only visual senses were involved, potentially leading to a weaker sense of experience in the office context.
Future research should incorporate other forms of sensory evaluation (e.g., touch, smell) to improve comprehensiveness and objectivity.
Future studies could use immersive helmets/glasses and tactile gloves to enhance the experience of wooden spaces.
Future studies could include eye-movement and EEG experiments to further explore sensory evaluation, affective responses, and tendency to act.
